blocks.text: Put an aluminium spoon and the same mass of water on the same stove for one minute. The spoon becomes too hot to hold; the water is barely warm. Water needs almost five times as much energy per kilogram for each degree of rise — and that single fact explains car radiators, sea breezes and why boiling a pot of soup takes so long.

blocks.title: Heat capacity and specific heat capacity
blocks.text: The heat capacity C of a body is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of the WHOLE body by one kelvin, measured in J K⁻¹. The specific heat capacity c of a substance is the heat required to raise the temperature of ONE KILOGRAM of it by one kelvin, measured in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. The two are linked by C = mc.

blocks.caption: Heat supplied = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change

blocks.markdown: Because a **temperature change** of 1 K is exactly the same size as a change of $1\ ^\circ\text{C}$, you may substitute a temperature *difference* in either unit without converting. Only absolute temperatures themselves need converting, and that arises in the gas laws, not here.

blocks.caption: Standard values. Water's unusually high value is the one you must remember.

blocks.title: Heating water in a kettle
blocks.prompt: Calculate the heat energy needed to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C. Take the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

steps.text: Write the formula for heat supplied.
Find the temperature change. A change in °C equals the same change in kelvin.
Substitute the mass, specific heat capacity and temperature change.
State the answer, converting to a convenient unit.

blocks.markdown:
### The method of mixtures

When a hot body and a cold body are mixed in a well-insulated container, no heat escapes to the surroundings, so

$$\text{heat lost by the hotter body} = \text{heat gained by the cooler body}$$

Write both sides using $mc\,\Delta\theta$, with the **final common temperature** $\theta$ appearing in each. The hotter body's change is $(\theta_{\text{hot}} - \theta)$ and the cooler body's is $(\theta - \theta_{\text{cold}})$ — both written so that each is positive.

blocks.title: Mixing hot and cold water
blocks.prompt: 0.50 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 1.50 kg of water at 20 °C in a well-lagged container. Calculate the final temperature of the mixture.

steps.text: Let the final common temperature be θ. Write the heat lost by the hot water.
Write the heat gained by the cold water.
Set them equal. The specific heat capacity 4200 appears on both sides and cancels.
Collect the θ terms on one side and the numbers on the other.
Divide to find the final temperature.
Sense-check: the answer lies between 20 °C and 80 °C, and closer to 20 °C because there is three times as much cold water.

items: Water is used in car radiators and engine cooling because its high specific heat capacity lets it absorb a lot of heat for a small temperature rise.
The sea warms and cools far more slowly than the land, which drives land and sea breezes along the Nigerian coast.
Cooking pots are made of metals with low specific heat capacity so they heat up quickly.
Hot-water bottles work well because water stores a large amount of heat and releases it slowly.
In the laboratory, a calorimeter is lagged so that the heat lost to the surroundings is negligible.

blocks.title: Heat capacity is not specific heat capacity
blocks.text: Heat capacity C is a property of a particular object and has unit J K⁻¹; specific heat capacity c is a property of the material and has unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. A question that gives you "heat capacity 1800 J K⁻¹" already includes the mass, so use Q = C Δθ and do NOT multiply by the mass again.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: In method-of-mixtures questions, remember the calorimeter itself if the question gives its mass and material. Its heat capacity must be added to that of the water it contains, otherwise your final temperature will be slightly too high.

points: Heat capacity C is the heat needed to raise a whole body by 1 K, in J K⁻¹; specific heat capacity c refers to 1 kg, in J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
C = mc, and heat supplied is Q = mc Δθ.
A temperature difference in °C equals the same difference in kelvin, so no conversion is needed for Δθ.
Water's specific heat capacity of 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is unusually high, which makes it an excellent coolant.
In the method of mixtures, heat lost by the hot body equals heat gained by the cold body in a lagged container.
